Main article: [Enlargement of NATO](/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO "Enlargement of NATO")

NATO was established on 4 April 1949 via the signing of the [North Atlantic Treaty](/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty "North Atlantic Treaty") (Washington Treaty). The 12 founding members of the Alliance were: [Belgium](/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), [Canada](/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Denmark](/wiki/Denmark "Denmark"), France, [Iceland](/wiki/Iceland "Iceland"), [Italy](/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Luxembourg](/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg"), the [Netherlands](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), [Norway](/wiki/Norway "Norway"), [Portugal](/wiki/Portugal "Portugal"), the United Kingdom, and the United States.[[4]](#cite_note-Members-4)

The various allies all signed the Ottawa Agreement,[[5]](#cite_note-Mosquera_2019-5) which is a 1951 document that acts to embody civilian oversight of the Alliance.[[5]](#cite_note-Mosquera_2019-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Current membership consists of 32 countries. In addition to the 12 founding countries, four new members joined during the Cold War: [Greece](/wiki/Greece "Greece") and [Turkey](/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") (1952), [West Germany](/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany") (1955) and [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain") (1982). Additionally, NATO experienced territorial expansion during this period without adding new member states when [Zone A of the Free Territory of Trieste](/wiki/Free_Territory_of_Trieste#Dissolution "Free Territory of Trieste") was annexed by Italy in 1954, and the territory of the former [East Germany](/wiki/East_Germany "East Germany") was added with the [reunification of Germany](/wiki/German_reunification "German reunification") in 1990. A typical set of polyhedral dice in various colors. They consist of the five Platonic solids, along with a ten-sided die that is also used for generating percentages.

Various shapes such as two-sided or four-sided dice are documented in archaeological findings; for example, from Ancient Egypt and the Middle East. While the cubical six-sided die became the most common type in many parts of the world, other shapes were always known, like 20-sided dice in Ptolemaic and Roman times.

The modern tradition of using *sets* of polyhedral dice started around the end of the 1960s when non-cubical dice became popular among players of [wargames](/wiki/Wargame "Wargame"),[[32]](#cite_note-Peterson2012-32) and since have been employed extensively in [role-playing games](/wiki/Role-playing_game "Role-playing game") and [trading card games](/wiki/Collectible_card_game "Collectible card game"). Dice using both the numerals 6 and 9, which are reciprocally symmetric through rotation, typically distinguish them with a dot or underline.

Some twenty-sided dice have a different arrangement used for the purpose of keeping track of an integer that counts down, such as health points. These *spindown dice* are arranged such that adjacent integers appear on adjacent faces, allowing the user to easily find the next lower number. They are commonly used with [collectible card games](/wiki/Collectible_card_game "Collectible card game").[[33]](#cite_note-33)

Main article: [Spain at the UEFA European Championship](/wiki/Spain_at_the_UEFA_European_Championship "Spain at the UEFA European Championship")

Spain have won the most UEFA European Championships, with four titles.[[108]](#cite_note-110) *La Roja* are also the only nation to date to have won consecutive championships. They have hosted the tournament once, in [1964](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1964 "UEFA Euro 1964") (one city was used to host games at [Euro 2020](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2020 "UEFA Euro 2020")) and have appeared in a total of twelve tournaments.

The team won their first international trophy on home soil in 1964, defeating the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union_national_football_team "Soviet Union national football team") 2–1.[[109]](#cite_note-111)[[110]](#cite_note-112) Spain would reach the final twenty years later in [1984](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1984_final "UEFA Euro 1984 final"), where they would lose the final to [France](/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team"). Spain would not reach the final again until [2008](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2008_final "UEFA Euro 2008 final"), where they would defeat Germany 1–0. Four years later, Spain earned back-to-back titles, comprehensively defeating [Italy](/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team") 4–0 in the [final](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2012_final "UEFA Euro 2012 final") in Kyiv.

It would take *La Roja* twelve years to reach another European final, doing so in [2024](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2024_final "UEFA Euro 2024 final") against [England](/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team"), a match they won 2–1 to stand alone as the most successful national team in the competition's history with four titles, while at the same time becoming the first team ever to win all seven matches in a single tournament.[[111]](#cite_note-113)
